items.body: Review by bandtutu — Drowning Steps - The Bravery of a Tireless Mind: Book One1. The Angels and the PlaygroundThe Angels and the Playground is an excellent introduction to the album. I really like the way it begins to develop the character's story. One detail I particularly love is the sound of the pencil writing on paper. It may seem like something simple, but it really adds to the immersion in the narrative. Caio's vocals also deserve praise, as they fit the song's concept very well and help convey the emotions behind the story.The first three minutes are beautiful. The acoustic guitar is very well crafted, and the atmosphere at the beginning reminds me of moments from "The Moon Touches Your Shoulder" by Porcupine Tree and "A Pillow of Winds" by Pink Floyd. There is a nostalgic tranquility to this introduction that I really enjoy, with a delicate arrangement that allows each element to find its own space. The song progresses naturally, without rushing, and never becomes tedious.Around 4:15, we get an incredible transition. The guitar riff, accompanied by the keyboards and synthesizers, changes the whole dimension of the composition and creates one of the first major moments of the song. I really like how these elements complement each other. The acoustic guitar picking that comes in here, breaking up the rhythm, also deserves praise.At 6:30, the distorted guitar introduces a section that, although I understand its importance to the narrative and the character's emotional context, buy simply doesn't work for me. I really don't like the riff. I understand the intention behind the change and recognize its purpose within the song, but I feel another approach could have conveyed the same feeling in a better way. It's a very personal criticism, especially because the composition wins me back shortly afterward.At 7:37, another guitar riff comes in, accompanied by the synthesizer, and the result is excellent. The drums also deserve praise, as the changes in the groove give the composition more personality. I really like the bass's rich and distinctive tone, and for me, this combination works so well that it makes up for much of what bothered me in the previous section.At 9:07, after a very striking, almost ghostly break, the song moves into a section that reminds me of "Moonloop" by Porcupine Tree. Even though this is a relatively long passage, it never becomes tedious. The instrumental development keeps me interested and shows the band's ability to sustain extended sections without simply relying on the repetition of the same idea.At 10:47, a riff with a more metal feel begins to emerge. I can't quite define exactly what kind of sound it is, but I really like the change. It's the kind of riff I would even like to write myself, both because of its sound and the energy it carries. Just a few seconds later, at 11:02, another transition completely changes the emotional state of the song. The arrangement takes on a different dimension, setting the stage for one of my favorite moments of the track.The keyboards entering at 11:23 are simply incredible. The piano comes in with a very emotional quality, adding a special sensitivity to everything that had been building up until that point. This section really moved me, especially because of the way the instrument transforms the atmosphere without needing an exaggerated change in intensity. Thiago's work on the keyboards is fundamental here, showing how important his contributions are to the musical identity of both the song and the album.When everything seems to be heading toward a satisfying conclusion, the guitar comes back and creates a sudden shock that, interestingly enough, works very well for me. I don't see this choice as a problem, in fact, I really like the effect it creates.However, my biggest criticism comes right after that, at 12:27, when the previously used riff returns. I feel that bringing it back is unnecessary and slightly hurts the flow of the composition. In my opinion, the song had already found an interesting path toward its conclusion, and I didn't like going back to that idea.Still, I really like the grandiose effect created by the keyboards together with the vocals during the "Then we went up, then we went down" section. The combination has a lot of strength and fits the scale of the narrative, although the repetition of this passage became a little boring for me. The ending of the section, with the guitar delay, works well and sets the stage for the final part of the song.The final section is beautiful. After so many changes in intensity and instrumental passages, the song finally reaches a sense of peace that almost feels like a release. The atmosphere reminds me a lot of "Insurgentes" by Steven Wilson. It also gives me the same feeling of relief I get when "Raider II" ends and "Like Dust I Have Cleared from My Eye" begins on Grace for Drowning. After such a long emotional journey, it feels like you can finally breathe.Despite some choices that don't completely work for me, "The Angels and the Playground" is a very strong opening, with excellent instrumental moments, engaging dynamic shifts, and an atmosphere that contributes just as much to the musical experience as it does to the narrative.------------------------------------2. Fragments of a LifetimeI found this song quite interesting, especially because it takes a very different approach from the previous track. It has this kind of progressive folk-ballad feel, with a very atmospheric arrangement. The keyboard effects also remind me a lot of "Entangled" by Genesis, and I think they fit the song really well.I also really liked the ending, when the song starts to give you the feeling that something is going wrong. It's an interesting choice because it works as a lead-in to the next track, "The Nod", leaving a certain sense of tension in the air.I like the idea behind the lyrics, especially this moment where the character is searching for peace. Overall, it's a simple track, but it works really well within the story of the album. --------------------------3. The NodThe beginning of this song reminds me a lot of Opeth atmosphere. Then a very distinctive guitar riff comes in. I wouldn't necessarily say it's good or bad, but I understand the idea behind it and I think it works.I really like the part around 2:35, when a sequenced drum pattern starts playing in the background. I thought that was a very interesting choice, and it reminds me of some things Wilson has done. The drums also deserve some praise here; they give the song a lot of dynamics and help build that sense of tension without simply making everything heavy all the time.The bass solo is also really good, especially with the character's narration playing in the background. Then the heavy guitar riff from the beginning comes back, and this time I think it really gains more meaning and fits the song very well.I also really liked the synthesizer solo, which brings a different texture to the track. The guitar solo is good as well and works nicely within the composition.Overall, I think the song takes its time to show this depth and develop the idea further.----------------------------------------------4. Waiting for RedemptionThis is easily my favorite song on the album. It starts with a piano in the background and Caio's vocals, which once again deserve a lot of praise. I really like how the song gradually builds along with the lyrics, creating more and more tension as it progresses.The way the song keeps building gives me a strong Neal Morse vibe. I can't really say whether it reminds me more of Transatlantic, Spock's Beard, or his solo work, but there is definitely something about the way the song develops that makes me think of those bands.Around 3:50, a guitar riff comes in and fits the song really well. The effects also deserve a lot of praise here. They manage to create a completely different atmosphere and then return to the previous one in a very natural way, without making the transitions feel forced.This particular riff really reminds me of a riff from the bridge of "Weenie Beenie," from Foo Fighters first album. It's not exactly the same, of course, but the way the riff comes in gives me a very similar feeling.Then, around 5:15, the song goes through a complete change. Once again, it shifts into a darkness and more introspective atmosphere.Shortly after that, the synthesizer solo comes in, and together with the drums, it sounds incredible. Listening to it gives me a really good feeling, almost as if I'm going on a trip. And maybe that's exactly what the character is experiencing in the story as well.Then that heavy riff comes back, this time accompanied by a wah-wah guitar solo, and I absolutely love it. It's really spectacular. The combination of the riff, the guitar tone, and the wah-wah works incredibly well.A new verse then comes in, very well placed, followed by the return of that almost ghostly section, which keeps repeating.My only real criticism is that this final part starts to feel a repetitive. I like the atmosphere it creates, but I think it goes on a little longer than it should.Even so, this is easily the track that stands out the most to me. It has so many great ideas that fit together really well, and the way it moves between different atmospheres while maintaining the narrative is excellent.----------------------------5. Life Handed Me the MapThis is the song that closes the album. It feels like the character is expressing his gratitude for having finally found the path; the "map", that will allow him to reconnect with the fragments of his past.I really like the effects and the atmosphere of the song. There is something very calm and reflective about it, which makes it feel appropriate as the ending of the story.I also really like the detail of hearing him write again at the end of the song, followed by the sound of the book closing. I think it's a great way to bring the album to an end, especially because the sound of the pencil writing appeared earlier in the story. It gives the whole thing a feeling of closure, almost as if we've just finished reading the character's story ourselves.--------------Overall Opinion on the AlbumFor me, this is a work that shows how much the band has matured, both in their songwriting and in the way they tell their story. I really enjoyed the songs, especially the way the album manages to create different atmospheres and make them work within the narrative.The main highlights for me were The Angels and the Playground, The Nod, and especially Waiting for Redemption. Overall, this is an album that really surprised me and shows how much Drowning Steps has evolved. It's a record I definitely plan to listen to over and over again, because I feel like there are still a lot of details to discover.-----------My Ratings:4,3/5 8,6/10Congratulations for this excellent work.Caio Claro / vocals, acoustic guitar (1), guitars (2,5), Arrangements and Sound ManipulationFabricio Mendon�a / drumsLeonardo Gon�alves / bassMarcos Duran / guitars (1-4)Tiago Pierucci / keyboards, synthesizers, effects, organ, piano, Wah-Wah guitar (2), backing vocals (4), Arrangements and Sound ManipulationRobin Peachey / vocals (1)La�s Gonzalez / vocals (2)Erlend Viken / vocals (3)

items.body: Independent Polish musician Sławek Stróżyk released the single “Tylko Ty” (“Only You”) on September 18, 2026, through distributor Crave Digital. The track places Polish-language male vocals in a synthwave/electro setting with a cyberpunk atmosphere, and explores closeness as a source of strength while the surrounding world changes. “Tylko Ty” runs 2 minutes and 47 seconds at 120 BPM. Stróżyk wrote the composition and lyrics, performed the track and handled its recording, production, mix and master himself in his home studio using Reaper. The original music and vocals involved no generative AI. “Tylko Ty” previously featured on the “Synthpop Symphony” podcast. The single is available to stream on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. About Sławek Stróżyk Sławek Stróżyk is an independent musician, composer, guitarist, vocalist and producer based in Poznań, Poland, with more than twenty years of experience spanning session performance, recording engineering and sound design. His solo work brings together synthwave and electronic production with a wider interest in pop, ballads and rock. Stróżyk records in his own home studio using Reaper, taking responsibility for the complete creative and technical process from composition through to the finished master. “Tylko Ty,” released September 18, 2026, is his latest single under that approach. Stróżyk is currently working on his debut solo album, with material spanning pop, ballads, rock and synthwave, continuing the independent, self-produced method behind “Tylko Ty.”

items.body: Sydney-based producer Harry Klein released the single “Fleeting Moments” in 2026, a dark-pop track built from electronica, wave and witch house. The song centers on transience, and on learning to love what doesn’t last. “Fleeting Moments” runs 3:22 and carries a synthesized trumpet line, falsetto vocals and a glitch beat. The single adds to a run of 2026 releases that includes “Push and Pull,” “Only Ever Now,” “Dance Therapy,” “Sun Down” featuring Billsbry, “Wild Child” and “Refuge” featuring Just Jen. Klein is touring Europe with psych-jazz outfit Almost Toast and plans to release his second album, “On The Path,” in November 2026 after he returns to Sydney. Rex Pollard of Electronic Music Australia described Klein’s production in terms of the mood it builds: “It is clear to me that Klein contains excellent knowledge on formulating dystopian atmospheres with his production, encouraging listeners to exit reality and enter his dark, sinister worlds.” “Fleeting Moments” is available to stream on Spotify. About Harry Klein Harry Klein is a multidisciplinary artist based in Eora/Sydney who combines music production with visual artistry across audio/visual performances. His work moves through dark electronica, glitchy IDM beats and ambient textures. Klein released his debut album, “And Then There Was None,” in 2023. The record explores questions of relationships, community and social power, pairing experimental electronica and dance productions with melancholic pop songwriting. Three singles preceded it that year: “Running out of Time,” “Cut & Dirty” and “Accelerate,” followed later in 2023 by “Who Floats Above.” He has performed at Up Late at the Powerhouse Museum and the Brand X Artist Showcase, built an interactive sound installation at Wide Open Space Festival, played his festival debut at Waves Retreat Festival and collaborated with fashion label The Injury at Pitch Festival. Klein also works as Senior Technical Officer of Screen Arts and Photomedia at Sydney College of the Arts, where he teaches and mentors emerging artists. “Fleeting Moments” is the latest in a string of 2026 singles building toward “On The Path,” Klein’s second album, due in November 2026.

items.body: Kontravoid has announced an extensive European run for November and December 2026, combining support dates with Boy Harsher and Choir Boy, a stop at Hellsinki Industrial Festival, a series of headline shows and a final stretch alongside Los Angeles EBM duo Spike Hellis. The tour also includes three Polish dates in Warsaw, Kraków and Poznań. The tour arrives just weeks after Kontravoid released the new ten-track album “Sound of the Void” on 2 October through Artoffact Records. The record follows 2024’s “Detachment” and includes tracks such as “Mortal”, “Chances”, “Returning” and the title track. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid The first part of the European run begins on 14 November at Le Transbordeur in Lyon, where Kontravoid joins Boy Harsher and Choir Boy. Dates follow in Paris, Strasbourg, Frankfurt, Lausanne, Munich and Vienna. Boy Harsher’s own schedule confirms Choir Boy across these European shows. Kontravoid then breaks away on 21 November for Hellsinki Industrial Festival, where the Saturday bill also includes Gothminister, Das Ich, Ambassador21 and others. After further headline dates through Greece, Italy and Switzerland, Kontravoid returns in December for another run, this time with Spike Hellis. That section reaches Hamburg, Copenhagen, Berlin and then Poland, with shows at Mechanik in Warsaw on 11 December, Gwarek in Kraków on 12 December and Pod Minogą in Poznań on 13 December. The Poznań date is already confirmed as a Kontravoid and Spike Hellis bill, while the Kraków show has also gone on sale as part of the Europe Fall 2026 tour. Tour dates for Kontravoid 14.11 – Lyon, FR – Le Transbordeur * 15.11 – Paris, FR – Bataclan * 16.11 – Strasbourg, FR – La Laiterie * 17.11 – Frankfurt, DE – Zoom * 18.11 – Lausanne, CH – Docks * 19.11 – Munich, DE – Kesselhaus * 20.11 – Vienna, AT – Ottakringer Brauerei * 21.11 – Helsinki, FI – Hellsinki Industrial Festival 23.11 – Thessaloniki, GR – The Host 24.11 – Athens, GR – Death Disco 26.11 – Pisa, IT – Caracol 27.11 – Bologna, IT – Freakout 28.11 – Messina, IT – Retronouveau 30.11 – Zurich, CH – Xtra-Musikcafé 05.12 – Rotterdam, NL – Baroeg ** 06.12 – Paris, FR – Le Chinois ** 08.12 – Hamburg, DE – MS Stubnitz ** 09.12 – Copenhagen, DK – BETA ** 10.12 – Berlin, DE – Cassiopeia ** 11.12 – Warsaw, PL – Mechanik ** 12.12 – Kraków, PL – Gwarek ** 13.12 – Poznań, PL – Pod Minogą ** * with Boy Harsher and Choir Boy ** with Spike Hellis About Kontravoid Kontravoid is the solo project of Cameron Findlay, mixing darkwave, EBM, industrial electronics and club music. Findlay’s masked live presence has become part of the project’s visual identity, but the music stays built for direct physical impact: rigid bass sequences, heavy electronic percussion and melodies that often cut through the harsher production with unusual clarity. “Sound of the Void” is Kontravoid’s second full-length for Artoffact Records and contains ten tracks. Kontravoid’s North American tour with Buzz Kull ran earlier in 2026, and Side-Line covered the new album’s announcement in September (Kontravoid announces new album ‘Sound Of The Void’, shares single ‘Without’) ahead of its 2 October release (Kontravoid releases new album ‘Sound Of The Void’). About Boy Harsher Boy Harsher, the duo of Jae Matthews and Augustus Muller, enter the European dates with a new album of their own. “GET MEAN” was released on 18 September 2026 and contains twelve tracks. The record deals directly with grief, heartbreak and survival. It keeps the duo’s characteristic combination of minimal electronics, coldwave and physically insistent club rhythms. Their European tour begins in Lyon on 14 November and continues through France, Germany, Switzerland, Austria, the Netherlands and the UK. About Choir Boy Choir Boy began as the project of vocalist and songwriter Adam Klopp, with the current line-up also including Chaz Costello, Jeff Kleinman and Michael Paulsen. The band’s sound sits on the softer edge of the tour’s spectrum, built from dream pop, new wave and romantic synth-pop. In April 2026 they released the single “I’ll Always Let You Down”, written by the full band with Jorge Elbrecht and described by Klopp as an “anti-love song”. About Spike Hellis Los Angeles duo Spike Hellis bring the December dates back toward harsher body music. Their second full-length, “Successor”, was released on 7 August 2026 and follows their 2022 self-titled debut. The ten-track record includes “By God”, “Your Successor”, “Unwound (Get Right)” and “Entirely Mine”. It keeps the duo’s stripped, physical combination of EBM, industrial electronics and minimal synth. The duo describe their sound as “body music to hijack the amygdala.”

items.body: Los Angeles darkwave trio Chalice Sect released its first EP, “Finis Initii”, on September 25, 2026. The four-track release combines two new songs with two previously issued singles, among them “Silent Fever,” released in March 2026. The EP’s four tracks move between post-punk, EBM and dark electro. Its title translates from Latin as “the end of the beginning.” Daniel of Chalice Sect describes the release as closing the project’s early period: “Finis Initii – Latin for ‘the end of the beginning’ – represents the closing of the first chapter of Chalice Sect. The EP brings together the remaining songs I wrote during that period but had not yet released, alongside the two previously released singles. These tracks were written over the past few years and belong to an earlier phase of the project, both creatively and sonically. Bringing them together on this release gives that era a proper conclusion while creating space for what comes next: a newer sound and perhaps a different direction for Chalice Sect.” Finis Initii by Chalice Sect The tracklist runs “Fire in the Sound,” “Silent Fever,” “Take Me There Parts I & II” and “Undefined.” “Finis Initii” is available as a digital release on Bandcamp and Spotify. About Chalice Sect Chalice Sect is a Los Angeles darkwave trio. The band released its debut single, “Violet Grey,” on January 20, 2026, followed by “Silent Fever” that March. “Finis Initii,” issued September 25, 2026 as the band’s first EP, gathers the project’s new and previously released material from that period into a single release. Press materials for “Finis Initii” cite Twin Tribes, Kontravoid, She Past Away and Molchat Doma as reference points for the band’s sound.

items.body: a-ha‘s second studio album, “Scoundrel Days,” turns 40 this year. The Norwegian band released the record on 6 October 1986 through Warner Bros. Records in the US, with WEA International handling distribution elsewhere. Recording took place in early 1986 at RG Jones Recording Studios in Wimbledon, south-west London. “Scoundrel Days” runs ten tracks and just under 39 minutes. Alan Tarney produced and mixed most of the album, while Magne Furuholmen and Pål Waaktaar self-produced “I’ve Been Losing You,” “Maybe, Maybe” and “Soft Rains of April.” Gerry Kitchingham engineered the sessions, with additional mixing by John Hudson. The tracklist runs “Scoundrel Days,” “The Swing of Things,” “I’ve Been Losing You,” “October,” “Manhattan Skyline,” “Cry Wolf,” “We’re Looking for the Whales,” “The Weight of the Wind,” “Maybe, Maybe” and “Soft Rains of April.” The album was preceded by the single “I’ve Been Losing You,” released on 22 September 1986, which reached number one in Norway and number eight in the UK. “Cry Wolf” followed on 24 November 1986 and reached the top five in the UK, Poland and Ireland. “Manhattan Skyline” was issued as a single in February 1987, peaking at number 13 in the UK. “Scoundrel Days” reached number one in Norway and number two on the UK Albums Chart, and was certified platinum in the UK, Germany, Switzerland, France, New Zealand and Norway. Rhino Records released an expanded two-disc edition on 6 July 2010, adding extended mixes, demos, B-sides and live tracks. About a-ha a-ha formed in Oslo, Norway, in 1982 as a trio of Morten Harket on vocals, Magne Furuholmen on keyboards and Pål Waaktaar on guitars. Warner Bros. Records signed the band, and a-ha released its debut album, “Hunting High and Low,” in 1985. The title track and “Take On Me” became international hits, the latter reaching number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 in October 1985. The band returned to RG Jones Recording Studios in Wimbledon in early 1986 to record its follow-up, “Scoundrel Days,” released on 6 October 1986. a-ha continued with “Stay on These Roads” (1988), “East of the Sun, West of the Moon” (1990) and “Memorial Beach” (1993) before going on hiatus. The group reformed in the late 1990s and released “Minor Earth Major Sky” (2000), “Lifelines” (2002), “Analogue” (2005), “Foot of the Mountain” (2009), “Cast in Steel” (2015) and “True North” (2022). The current touring lineup adds Karl-Oluf Wennerberg on drums and Erik Ljunggren on keyboards, both since 2009, and Even Ormestad on bass since 2015. Forty years after its release, “Scoundrel Days” remains the second entry in a catalogue that now spans eleven studio albums.

items.body: Claudio Dondo began making music in the late 1980s. This path eventually led him to Runes Order, the project under which he has released countless recordings on a wide variety of labels since 1992. He has now joined forces with the German label Dark Vinyl Records and, much like on his previous album, initiated a collaboration with Regen Graves. We are presented with a total of 13 tracks. While the influences are highly eclectic, they can largely be categorized within genres such as Cinematic and Krautrock. The inclusion of additional guest musicians adds further diversity—for instance, on one track, a saxophone creates a wonderfully dark, Jazzy atmosphere. I wasn’t surprised to find references to John Carpenter’s films, yet this album offers far more than just Cinematic soundscapes. From vintage drum machine tones to driving rhythms, and from organ passages to analog effects, this work has a great deal to offer. Add to this a variety of vocal tracks alongside the instrumentals, and the result is a fascinating work that keeps the listener firmly in its grip. This is a varied and accomplished opus containing a few real gems. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Bury The Fetus”: Bury The Fetus by Runes Order & Regen Graves About Runes Order & Regen Graves Runes Order & Regen Graves is the collaboration between Claudio Dondo’s long-running Italian dark ambient project Runes Order, based in the Genoa area, and Regen Graves, a musician from the same Genoa scene known as a member of the horror-doom band Abysmal Grief. Dondo started the project in 1988 as Order 1968 and renamed it Runes Order in 1992 with the cassette “The Dream Door”. His catalogue includes “La Seduzione Del Silenzio” (1994), “Room 39” (1995), “The Art of Scare and Sorrow” (2002) and “Fase XIV” (2019), drawing on the cosmic and Berlin School tradition of Tangerine Dream, Faust and Klaus Schulze. Dondo and Regen Graves first joined forces on “Falsche Fragen” in 2023. “Escape”, their second album together, followed in 2026 on Dark Vinyl Records, pairing Berlin School electronics with horror and thriller soundtrack atmospheres across the thirteen tracks reviewed here.

items.body: Turn it off, this channel’s boring, see? This is not how my life was supposed to be So I take this poison inside of me There is a delicious stupidity in trying to escape a miserable situation by making choices almost guaranteed to leave you worse off. The promise of feeling alive again has filled bars, emptied bank accounts, inspired regrettable phone calls, and sent countless people back into relationships they had good reason to leave. New England darkwave outfit Ghost Painted Sky have built Kissing Lions around one of humanity’s more dependable talents: recognizing the jaws directly in front of us and deciding, against every scrap of available evidence, to lean closer anyway. Taken from the forthcoming Failure Blooms, the song captures those moments when boredom and disappointment have accumulated enough weight that almost any escape starts to look reasonable, including the varieties with sharp teeth. The band began in Massachusetts in 2014 as David Strong’s project, expanding into a genuine partnership when vocalist and lyricist Lisa Wood joined in 2018. Guitarist Michael Boudreau followed in 2022, while longtime collaborator Aurora Grabill adds violin here and elsewhere on the album. What they produce on “Kissing Lions” belongs comfortably within darkwave and post-punk, though its real engine is psychological: the familiar urge to make some reckless little bargain with yourself because ordinary life has become intolerably beige. Wood sings from inside that bargain. The rising tide gets pushed away, the television gets switched off, poison gets swallowed, and eventually the lion receives a kiss directly on the mouth. You can practically hear the terrible idea becoming attractive in real time. The metaphor works because lions remain perfectly innocent in this arrangement. They were always going to bite. The speaker is the one grabbing the teeth. “Kissing Lions describes those mostly vain attempts to seize on anything that creates a fleeting feeling of being alive for a moment amid relentless waves of the humdrum, doldrums, and failure, which so often end up being misguided and ultimately just creating a thicker mire even more strangling than the original situation one sought to escape… bad decisions that bite back and create further downward spirals,” says Strong. Strong’s accompanying video stretches that idea across generations, combining 8mm footage shot by his grandfather, Herbert Virta, with material from a 2023 virtual performance for Goths for Sanctuaries and footage from The Heavy Culture Cooperative in Easthampton, Massachusetts, filmed in August 2026 with projected visuals by Daisy. Past and present collide without becoming sentimental window dressing; time simply keeps advancing while people continue finding increasingly elaborate ways to get bitten. Watch the video for Kissing Lions below: The digital maxi-single adds the brighter Kissing Lions (Effervescent Remix) and My Words Are Not My Own, which turns toward conformity and the slow surrender of individual voice. Mixed and mastered by William Faith, Failure Blooms follows 2018’s Flightless. Eight years later, Ghost Painted Sky sounds preoccupied with failure less as an ending than as a remarkably fertile place to keep making the same disastrous choices. Listen to Kissing Lions below and order the single here. items.body: I had hoped to be seen by you Unbroken gaze like a sweet arrow Could you ever feel my eyes on you Bathing you in my desire Desire has a way of making the body speak before the mind has decided what to say: flushed cheeks, an aching chest, the unreasonable hope that somebody might feel a glance from across the room. In the video for Sacred Hearts, Gloria de Oliveira takes those private sensations onto the streets of Hamburg’s St. Pauli district, where barroom lamps, photo-booth portraits, and the company of women give longing somewhere to live. The song’s burning heart finds a fitting companion in the red lights overhead, while affection passes between its subjects through looks, laughter, and the small pleasure of being together. The Berlin-based German-Brazilian musician and visual artist shares the video for the third single from her forthcoming album The Lying Swans, due October 30, 2026, through La Double Vie and Cargo Records. Produced by Randall Dunn, whose work includes records with Anna von Hausswolff and Marissa Nadler, Sacred Hearts considers the exhilaration and anxiety of giving yourself over to another person, particularly when the body seems to have made that decision ahead of you. The opening guitar figures carry an almost medieval character, joined by bright, percussive tones with the delicacy of a hammered dulcimer. Matt Chamberlain’s drumming briefly suggests the forward motion of Kate Bush’s Running Up That Hill before settling into the song’s own gait. Deep resonant strings lend the arrangement weight, while synthesizers soften its edges and extend its peculiar, old-world atmosphere. The tones and melody evoke a folk ballad like Nick Cave’s The Weeping Song, with the spaciousness of a Western just beyond the song’s antique ornamentation. De Oliveira sings into that space with a delicate quiver that evokes Elizabeth Fraser, with a classical poise softened by the intimacy of her delivery. Lennard Zander’s acoustic, electric, and 12-string guitars trace fine melodic lines without disturbing the vocal’s tenderness; Arjan Miranda anchors the arrangement on bass, while de Oliveira, Dunn, and Úlfur Hansson add layers of synthesizer. The music leaves her exposed yet almost weightless, as if every declaration of love might tip her toward losing her footing. The lyrics measure desire through its physical symptoms, moving from fever and sleeplessness toward the hope contained in a hand’s touch. To be seen becomes as urgent as to be loved, and the repeated attempts to contain that feeling only reveal its scale. Yet, the song’s title draws on an image de Oliveira has carried since childhood, joining religious devotion to the unruly sensations of romantic attachment. “The Catholic image of Christ’s Sacred Heart – a heart literally engulfed in flames – has struck me since childhood.” “Of course it’s meant to symbolise God’s boundless and passionate love for mankind – however, as John Keats once wrote, ‘I am certain of nothing but of the holiness of the heart’s affections, and the truth of imagination’. And how does it feel to give yourself over to that affection and desire despite fear? With this song, I wanted to capture these seemingly contrasting sentiments.” Shot and directed by award-winning Turkish filmmaker Seda Kaçak, and edited by de Oliveira, the video stars London actress Mona Najma alongside Eva Rogalla. Kaçak follows the women through St. Pauli in handheld close-ups, catching them sharing drinks, posing for photo-booth pictures, and moving between daylight streets and richly coloured interiors. Superimposed faces and starbursts around the lights give these ordinary pleasures an enchanted quality. Conceived as a homage to the bond between women, the film offers an affectionate counterpoint to the song’s solitary ache: companionship makes room for feelings that can otherwise become overwhelming. Watch the video for Sacred Hearts below: A classically trained singer whose acting work includes Babylon Berlin and Christian Petzold’s Undine, de Oliveira released music with the darkwave and synthpop duo lovespells before her 2020 debut album Fascination. Her 2022 collaboration with David Lynch’s longtime sound designer Dean Hurley, Oceans of Time, followed through Sacred Bones. Across those releases, she has explored dream pop, ethereal wave, ambient music, and the influence of her Brazilian roots, alongside work for theatre, film, and London Fashion Week. Recorded in Iceland, New York, and Berlin, The Lying Swans extends those interests across nine songs concerned with trauma, perception, and the difficult return of trust. Its title invokes the myth of Leda, while its literary references include John Keats, Emily Brontë, Anne Sexton, and Milton’s Paradise Lost. Within that broader examination of love and illusion, Sacred Hearts holds open the possibility of affection despite fear. Listen to Sacred Hearts below or via streaming services, and pre-order The Lying Swans here. The album is out October 30, 2026, on digital, vinyl, CD, and cassette. items.body: …O sun, that healest all distempered vision, thou dost content me so, when thou resolvest,that doubting pleases me no less than knowing! -Dante Alighieri, Divine Comedy Golden Apes have spent more than twenty years making music for people who think a bass guitar should sound slightly dangerous, a baritone ought to carry bad news with dignity, and every decent chorus deserves at least one guitar line large enough to knock over the furniture. On The Sun Came Up Tremendously, the Berlin band sounds completely at home with that assignment. Ten songs move between post-punk, dark wave, gothic rock, dreampop, and bruised alternative rock, yet the record never feels like a display cabinet of influences. Golden Apes know this country too well for tourism. They have lived here. There is plenty of history in these songs, of course. You can hear The Cure in the open space around certain guitar lines, Chameleons in the upward sweep of others, Cocteau Twins in the gauzier passages, and the severe romantic machinery of Clan of Xymox when the keyboards begin closing in. White Lies, Interpol, Lowlife, and The Horrors, drift through the bloodline. Yet Golden Apes have reached the point where influence is less a matter of borrowing than instinct. Twenty-plus years will do that to a band. Eventually your record collection gets absorbed into your nervous system. The Sun Came Up Tremendously follows 2024’s Our Ashes at the End of the Day as the second installment in a planned trilogy, with material written across 2024 and 2025 and recorded at Thommy Hein Studios in Berlin between late 2025 and early 2026. Thommy Hein also contributes guitar, joining vocalist and keyboardist Peer Lebrecht, guitarists Maximilian Hennig and Stephan Schoenfeld, bassist Christian Lebrecht, and drummer Salomon Bosse. The production favors size without polishing away the pressure inside these songs. Basslines keep pushing forward, drums give the record a stern physical gait, and the guitars are allowed to bloom, bruise, and occasionally swallow the room. Farewell begins with a plaintive guitar that sounds as if it’s emerging from a dream, and an open space that immediately calls The Chameleons to mind, though The Horrors’ later grandeur also shows in the way the arrangement keeps adding height. It is a lovely opening, sad without collapsing into self-pity, and expansive without turning into marble-statue rock. Peer Lebrecht sings as though he has already accepted whatever the song is grieving, which somehow makes the ache sharper. By the time the rhythm section settles in, the track feels less like a goodbye than the long walk away from one. The Light (Inside Us) comes on harder. The guitars widen, Christian Lebrecht’s bass digs in, and the verses carry a conversational quality before the chorus breaks open into a shoegaze-heavy rush. The seduction of scale takes center stage: the chorus is huge enough to make a ceiling seem temporarily optional, yet the band keeps enough dirt in the guitars to prevent grandeur from becoming ceremony. This is music reaching for the upper rows while keeping both boots on the club floor. Milk and Poison turns inward and drops the temperature. Its opening feels like ripples on water with dream-pop textures, though the song soon settles into an anthemic ballad buoyed by these currents, sailing on broad synth pads, acoustic accents, surging guitars, and Peer’s low, expressive voice. He has one of those voices that can make a grocery list sound vaguely incriminating, and Golden Apes wisely avoid burying it beneath unnecessary decoration. The arrangement gives him room, then closes around him in slow degrees. Resistance is where the record’s architecture comes into sharpest focus. A resonant guitar figure opens the track, answered by a low keyboard tone, as hi-hats hiss at the edges and the bass builds steady pressure. The arrangement grows heavier until the guitars reach the emotional scale of mid-eighties gothic rock. Peer remains composed as the band swells around him, and that restraint gives the song its authority. Near the center, a clean, melodic guitar solo arrives with almost startling simplicity, offering a brief clearing before the vocal returns with greater weight. No pyrotechnics are needed; the song already knows where its gravity lies. At intervals, the drums break into splashes and the rhythm pulls back, leaving more air around Peer’s euphoric delivery. The measured bass, sober guitar tone, and baritone gravity recall Scottish cult band Lowlife, while the surrounding textures remain recognizably Golden Apes. Helion heads toward the same terrain as Clan of Xymox and The Chameleons, with traces of Joy Division in its resigned vocals and the stern drive of its rhythm section. An emotional barrage of drums and surging guitars carries the song forward, giving its sense of exhaustion an almost overwhelming physical force. There is something perversely satisfying about how controlled it remains amid all that turbulence. Plenty of bands mistake gloom for permission to wallow; Golden Apes keep pushing through it. It is the sort of song you want to hear live, feel in your chest, and carry with you on the walk home after everybody else has disappeared. Where the River Ran slows the pace and brings Peer’s baritone into Nick Cave territory. The drums begin with a plodding military tattoo, giving the song a processional character, while guitar and synth gradually stretch outward until the arrangement takes on a shoegaze breadth. The transition works because the band allows it to happen patiently. What begins in discipline ends in something far less contained. Evelyn (One Day) opens with a long sigh, which is about as efficient a piece of scene-setting as anybody could ask for. The resemblance to Lowlife grows even stronger here, recalling the Scottish band at their most wistful, thoughtful, and romantic. Dream-pop synth textures surround Peer’s voice, while dramatic splashes of guitar and percussion accent the song’s tender emotion, not unlike The Cure’s “Push.” Once again, Golden Apes take the form of a ballad and keep expanding it until the walls seem to move outward. The song swells like the ocean, its quieter passages gathering strength before euphoric surges of guitar and drums break across the arrangement. Their fondness for large choruses could become ridiculous in less experienced hands, but the rhythm section keeps the drama tethered to muscle. Radiation opens with a steady drumbeat and dirgeful tones before Peer’s rich, deep baritone bellows with unusual force, almost thunderous without losing definition. The chiming guitars and rhythm section pull back to give him room, though the melodic bassline remains palpable, felt in the heart and bones. With the song’s titular refrain, a surge of guitars seems to radiate toward the fingertips, giving its emotional release a physical reach. The drums then quicken in anticipation, and the guitars sweep in sustained arcs before the refrain returns, each repetition gathering strength from the space the band leaves around the voice. City Walls slows everything again, returning to the Cave-like gravity heard earlier. The drums drag with deliberate weight while a manic hi-hat keeps scratching at the surface, and eerie female backing vocals add an uneasy human presence around Peer’s lead. The song feels boxed in by design. Space exists, but none of it seems comfortable. Every instrument appears to occupy its own corner while the room keeps shrinking. Then comes Dreams (Gone By), opening with strange industrial textures before a weighty rhythm section and eerie synth tones take control, recalling London After Midnight’s Kiss. The percussion has real physical heft, but the gloom gradually recedes as the song opens into the brighter dream-pop romance of Modern English and Lowlife. Golden Apes carry that change with the emotional swell established throughout the album, letting the arrangement expand without losing the force of its darker beginnings. A brief pause for a wistful guitar chime offers some breathing room before the gothic dance rhythm returns, subtly brighter now, and the song surges again. As a closer, it gives the album one last change in texture, moving from industrial unease toward romantic release while retaining the emotional weight of the previous nine tracks. By this point, the record has passed through goth, post-punk, dreampop, dark wave, and broad alternative rock without sounding indecisive. Golden Apes can write a severe club track, a huge guitar chorus, a graveyard ballad, or a slow piece that sounds built for stained glass and bad decisions, and somehow Peer Lebrecht’s voice keeps the record unified. His baritone carries longing, isolation, regret, and the occasional flash of release without turning every lyric into a public execution. There is drama here, plenty of it, but the band understands proportion. Even at their biggest, they leave enough space for the songs to breathe. The Sun Came Up Tremendously is also the work of a band with very little interest in pretending they discovered any of these styles yesterday. Golden Apes’ long touring history, including appearances at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Castle Party, and Murder of Crows, plus stages shared with The Chameleons, Pink Turns Blue, And Also the Trees, She Past Away, Whispering Sons, TRAITRS, Then Comes Silence, and others, has given them the practical education that comes from watching songs survive outside the studio. The title may promise sunrise, though nobody should expect birds chirping outside a kitchen window. Golden Apes prefer their light complicated, filtered through regret, desire, bad choices, and the stubborn suspicion that survival can occasionally be worth the inconvenience of a journey through hell and back. The only way to reach dawn, after all, is through the night. The Sun Came Up Tremendously is out now through Icy Cold Records. Listen to the album below and order here. items.body: Arcana Magna Silentia Cold Meat Industry The fourteen year gap between Swedish neo-classical/dark ambient project Arcana’s As Bright As A Thousand Suns and new LP Magna Silentia was marked by halted reactivations, live reunions, and tremendous personal loss for Peter and Cecilia Bjärgö and their collaborators. It’s no surprise, then, to find them working in a register quite different from their last recorded material, though Magna Silentia‘s combination of Arcana’s earliest and most austere work and the technical prowess they’ve since accrued makes for a striking and affecting reemergence. Records like Thousand Suns and Raspail saw an expansion of Arcana’s acoustic side, augmenting their neo-classical side with folk threads which resulted in a sound not unlike mid-period Dead Can Dance. That degree of ornamentation has been stripped back Magna Silentia. Low, abyssal horns and drones accompany ritual drums whose earthy timbre carries real menace on “The Adversity Bell”, yet the melodic thread of the piece, carried almost exclusively by Peter’s wordless vocals, is far more frail and pained than those more bracing elements might suggest. And it’s in that tension, between the severity of a record which fittingly marks Arcana’s return to Cold Meat Industry (and everything that infamous label entails) and the full, crushing emotional register of real human grief and loss, that Magna Silentia shines. A sustained focus on funereal dark ambient drones and echoes is often the conduit for that tension. Dark ambient has always been one part of Arcana’s heady alchemy to be sure, but it’s never been given so much focus as it has here. The rich sound design and subtle but elegant compositional chops which guide “Somnia Intus” might not have been achievable for Bjärgö in the project’s early years, but are now well within his grasp and fit the record’s sober and enduring grief. While perhaps more abstract and less directly emotional, “The Obsidian Mirror” again finds Arcana wielding both metallic, industrial noise and contemplative tones in equilibrium (for a project which has always focused on atmosphere they’ve rarely felt “cinematic” in the way that term’s often deployed, yet there’s something of a classic cyberpunk cityscape in this track). For all of its pain and extremity, there are real currents of beauty in Magna Silentia. The mournful violin which passes through glowing chorales in “The Collapsing Of All Light” might not be as bombastic as some of Arcana’s earlier neo-classical works, but it’s as affecting as any of them. After their hiatus Arcana have returned to their roots, shaped by time and loss, but none the weaker for it. Recommended. Buy it. items.body: Progressive rock can be defined in many ways but one of my favorites is with the tension between a frenetic, jittery energy and sweet, soothing melody. Think King Crimson, where you never know which the band will choose from and often get both: the staccato, chopped up riff, or the dreamy, pleasing melody. This creates a tension, a contrast between the two sounds that, when wielded well, generates an inimitable energy and mood. Sans Froid are experts at doing just that, marrying dense, complex, unpredictable instrumentation and unexpected vocal phrases with a "classic" melodic approach. The end result is Back Into the Womb, an album that covers the spaces between heavy, muscular progressive rock and fragile, warm art rock."Go On", the track which opens the album, leaves us very little space before it introduces the first aspect of this sound. This is the track's excellent combo of the main guitar riff, punchy drums, and punctual bass. It creates that off-kilter vibe I mentioned earlier, that jittery feeling. The vocals follow suit but also quickly usher in the other mood, a more classical, melodic kind of approach on the track's first bridge. But here's the thing - that back and forth is not maintained. There is no A/B/A/B/C structure to this track. It gets smashed to pieces by this sudden turn that the instruments and especially the vocals take around at two minutes and fifteen. It's hard to overstate how much I love what happens there: the initially repetitive but then exquisitely explosive vocals, the deconstructed guitar line, and then the return of the big, muscular main riff.The entire album is filled with these ideas, refusing to choose one style and instead hopping between groove, experimentation, emotiveness, abrasiveness and more. Throughout, the vocals lead the way. They're incredible, again channeling that contrast we opened on. Their basic timbre is very sweet but it often gets augmented by a throaty, full approach that works exceedingly well with the album's basic groove. But, as evinced on "Go On", Sans Froid are happy to manipulate them further, sometimes casting them in sweeping, "traditional" choruses and sometimes chopping them up and deploying them in non-standard ways while at others setting them as a melancholic, emotive, gentle dirge. The result is that their sound is the centerpiece of the album, tying everything together, but never becoming obvious or background noise.Which also brings us, at the outset, full circle to the album's other brilliance: its production. Every instrument is meticulously placed where it needs to be and even on the album's busiest passages, every comes through beautifully. The bass is at the bottom but it never slips, always audible in its support. The drums hit very hard right where they should without overwhelming anything else. And the guitars are at time noisy and beefy but at others poignantly sharp and incisiveness. It serves to bring Sans Froid's ambition, which is substantial, to exquisite execution, bringing forth the musical vision in beautiful light. Fans of progressive rock know how hard this is to achieve and also know the joy of discovering an album which does this well, an intricate album whose sound matches its composition. Back Into the Womb is that and more, an album from a band which I knew nothing about that does everything I love progressive rock for. Back into the Womb by Sans Froid

items.body: 2026.10.06 音楽家のための心身サポートと熟達支援を提供する「ミュージック・エクセレンス・トレーニングセンター」 このたび東京・五反田に、音楽家のための心身サポートと熟達支援を提供する、世界初の教育プラットフォーム「ミュージック・エクセレンス・トレーニングセンター（トレセン）」が誕生しました。これは、楽器演奏における身体の使い方の研究で世界の先端をいく古屋晋一さんが中心となって立ち上げたもの。およそ四半世紀にわたる研究をもとに、科学とテクノロジーを駆使した独自のプログラムが組まれています。この未来を先取りするような「トレセン」を訪れ、古屋さん及びチーフコーチに最新の設備やプログラム内容について伺いました。 取材・文 取材・文 長井進之介 ピアニスト/音楽ライター 国立音楽大学演奏学科鍵盤楽器専修（ピアノ）卒業、同大学大学院修士課程器楽専攻（伴奏）修了を経て、同大学院博士後期課程音楽学領域単位取得。在学中、カールスルーエ音楽大学... 詳しく見る 扉を開けると、2台のピアノと共に複数のカメラやディスプレイなどのハイテク機器が並ぶ空間が広がる。ここは古屋晋一さんが代表理事を務める一般社団法人NeuroPianoが開設した「ミュージック・エクセレンス・トレーニングセンター（以下：トレセン）」。 5年間にわたり実施されたピアノアカデミー＊の成果を発展させ、音楽家のための身体教育とトレーニングに特化した世界初の施設だ。スポーツ界では、オリンピック選手を支えるトレーニングセンターや専門スタッフが存在する。一方で音楽家には、そのような仕組みがほとんどない。 「身体の故障やメンタルの不調によって演奏活動を断念する方は少なくありません。文化を持続させるためには、音楽家自身を支える仕組みが必要です」。そう語る古屋さんは、「文化のSDGsを実現したい」という。音楽家が心身ともに健やかに成長し、生涯にわたって演奏活動を続けられる環境づくりをトレセンは目指している。 ＊ピアノアカデミー：ソニーコンピュータサイエンス研究所が10代のピアニストを対象に、身体教育と芸術教育を包括的に提供するピアノ教育プログラム。現在12歳で活躍中のピアニスト・天野薫さんは修了生のひとり 演奏者自身も気づいていない身体の使い方を テクノロジーで可視化 核となるのが、古屋さんが研究と教育実践をもとに体系化した身体教育カリキュラム「PEAC（Physical Education for Artists Curriculum）」。「なぜその問題が起きているのか」という原因に着目したアプローチを行っている。それを支えているのが、長年にわたる研究とテクノロジーだ。レッスン室には、姿勢や重心移動、鍵盤の動きを計測するセンサーやカメラが設置され、演奏者自身も気づいていない身体の使い方を可視化できる。 別室にはAIを活用した練習システムを備えたピアノを設置。演奏すると、指先の向きや鍵盤への入り方などについて具体的なアドバイスが表示される。5年間のピアノアカデミーで蓄積された指導データを基に、一人ひとりに合わせたフィードバックが行われる仕組みだ。 さらなる別室には、「外骨格ロボット」と呼ばれる指のトレーニング装置が。指に装着すると、ロボットが自動的にトリルや特定の指の組み合わせを高速で動かしていく。その際、自発的な動きはまったく必要とされない。複雑な運動パターンが何の無理もなく繰り返し体験できるのだ。古屋さんは、「これは筋力トレーニングではなく、脳のトレーニング」だという。効率的な運動学習を促す研究から生まれた技術であり、長時間の反復練習だけに頼らずに技術習得が促される。今回は短時間の体験だったが、装置を外したあと、指の動きの軽さを実感した。 「外骨格ロボット」を指に装着し、習得したい指の動きを入力すると、ロボットが勝手に動いてくれる。「安静にしているだけで大丈夫。脳がちゃんと学習してくれますよ」と古屋さん （古屋晋一：ソニーコンピューターサイエンス研究所 東京リサーチ リサーチディレクター、一般社団法人 NeuroPiano 代表理事、ハノーファー音楽演劇メディア大学 音楽生理学・音楽家医学研究所 客員教授、東京音楽大学 特任教授、他） 「PEAC」に基づくレッスンを体験！ 具体的なアドバイスで音が驚くほど変わる 続いて体験したのが、「PEAC」に基づくレッスンだ。まず筆者がショパンのエチュードの一節を演奏。その後、チーフコーチの塩木ももこさんが背中側から小さなボールを当て、「これを押し返すように意識してください」と声をかけられる。ボールを押し返そうとすると、自然と腹部や胴体で身体を支える感覚が生まれる。その状態でもう一度演奏すると、驚くほど音の響きが変わった。同じフレーズを弾いているにもかかわらず、音に厚みが増し、楽器全体がよく鳴るようになったのである。塩木先生によれば、「下半身や胴体が安定すると、指先が自由になり、音も変わる」のだそうだ。 さらに指先の方向や鍵盤への入り方についてアドバイスを受けると、わずかな身体の使い方の違いが音に直結することを実感できた。そして何より印象的だったのは、「こういう音を出したい」というイメージを実現するための具体的な手段が示されることだった。 姿勢や重心移動等の測定データが瞬時にスクリーン上で図示される。演奏者自身も気づいていない身体の使い方が可視化されることで、「なぜその問題が起きているのか」が具体的にわかり、「こういう音を出したい」というイメージを実現するための方法が示される 古屋さんは、「私たちがやりたいのは芸術表現を教えることではありません。どんな音を目指すのか、どんな表現をしたいのかを決めるのは、先生やアーティスト自身です。私たちは、その表現を実現するための身体の使い方や学び方を支えたいのです。フランス料理にたとえると、ヴィシソワーズ（ジャガイモの冷製スープ）を作るのは先生方の役割。その前にジャガイモの皮をむくことが、私たちの役割なのです」と話す。 演奏家が健やかに、豊かな表現を追求できる未来を目指すトレセン。取材を終えて強く感じたのは、ここで行われていることが「表現を支える」ということだった。その挑戦は、音楽家と音楽文化の未来を支える新しい一歩となりそうだ。 ミュージック・エクセレンス・トレーニングセンター 学習者向けコース ◆カリキュラムコース：演奏に必要な身体の基盤をつくる スケール・アルペジオコース 和音・オクターブコース items.body: 音楽家の三宅純がスコアを手がけた、映画『Oxygen Station（オキシジェン・ステーション）』のサウンドトラックがリリース決定。 映画『Oxygen Station』は、2023年に制作されたウクライナ、チェコ、スロバキア、スウェーデンの共同制作による伝記ドラマ映画で、クリミア・タタール民族指導者として知られるムスタファ・ジェミレフ（Mustafa Dzhemilev）の生涯が描かれている。 監督はウクライナのイヴァン・ティムチェンコ（Ivan Tymchenko）。本作でウクライナ最高峰の国家映画賞であるゴールド・ズィーガ賞や、 オデッサ国際映画祭などでも受賞を果たしている。   なお、2026年10月13日（火）には 晴れたら空に豆まいて（東京都渋谷区）にてトークイベント『三宅純の広告音楽 CM TRACKS vol.2』が開催される。同イベントは、三宅純がこれまでに手がけてきたCM音楽を「広告」というコンテクストから切り離し、純粋な音楽作品として掘り下げる企画で、三宅本人が楽曲を解説。『Oxygen Station』のサウンドトラックも試聴予定で、同作の音楽制作にまつわるエピソードも聞ける貴重な機会となる。 三宅純 / 『オキシジェン・ステーション』オリジナル・サウンドトラック 2026/10/09 発売 投稿 三宅純が手がけたウクライナ映画『Oxygen Station』オリジナル・サウンドトラックが配信リリース は ARBAN に最初に表示されました。

items.album: 山﨑健太｜『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』
items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 会期：2026/08/07〜2026/08/23 東京芸術劇場 シアターイースト［東京都］ 作・演出：岡田利規 公式サイト：https://www.geigeki.jp/performance/theater412/ 誰が舞台に立ち、誰が客席に座るのか。誰が誰を表象し、誰がそれを観るのか。『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』（作・演出：岡田利規）はそんな問いを改めて劇場へと持ち込み、そして観客に持ち帰らせるような作品だった。同作は岡田の東京芸術劇場舞台芸術部門芸術監督に就任第1作として上演されたもの。もともとはドイツのハノーファー州立劇場のレパートリーとして書かれ、5月に初演を迎えた岡田の現時点での最新作『Sliding Away』を、日本版の出演者・スタッフとともに新たに創り上げたものでもある。 タイトルが示す通り、舞台は映画を撮ろうとしているゾンビたちの撮影現場で展開する。登場するのは映画監督ゾンビのぽいぽい（東宮綾音）、俳優ゾンビのいいね（百瀬葉）、第5助監督ゾンビのまーしー（島田桃依）、第6助監督ゾンビのがーしー（石川朝日）、ゾンビ音楽家のげりま（福原冠）。しかし劇中で実際に映画の撮
items.body: 会期：2026/08/07〜2026/08/23 東京芸術劇場 シアターイースト［東京都］ 作・演出：岡田利規 公式サイト：https://www.geigeki.jp/performance/theater412/ 誰が舞台に立ち、誰が客席に座るのか。誰が誰を表象し、誰がそれを観るのか。『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』（作・演出：岡田利規）はそんな問いを改めて劇場へと持ち込み、そして観客に持ち帰らせるような作品だった。同作は岡田の東京芸術劇場舞台芸術部門芸術監督に就任第1作として上演されたもの。もともとはドイツのハノーファー州立劇場のレパートリーとして書かれ、5月に初演を迎えた岡田の現時点での最新作『Sliding Away』を、日本版の出演者・スタッフとともに新たに創り上げたものでもある。 タイトルが示す通り、舞台は映画を撮ろうとしているゾンビたちの撮影現場で展開する。登場するのは映画監督ゾンビのぽいぽい（東宮綾音）、俳優ゾンビのいいね（百瀬葉）、第5助監督ゾンビのまーしー（島田桃依）、第6助監督ゾンビのがーしー（石川朝日）、ゾンビ音楽家のげりま（福原冠）。しかし劇中で実際に映画の撮影が行なわれることはない。ゾンビたちは現場に集まったはいいものの、主要な俳優もスタッフもやってこないため撮影をはじめられない状況にあるのだ。かくして、時間を持て余したゾンビたちはゾンビが映画を撮ることに関する持論を交わしはじめる。 『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』東京芸術劇場（2026年8月）［撮影：銀色なつみ］ 冒頭からいいねは、ゾンビが人間を演じるための人間メイクをするのには3時間45分もかかる一方、「人間がゾンビになるときのメイクはもっとずっと短時間でテキトーに済ませたってオッケーってされてるんだから」その非対称性には許しがたいものがあるとぶち上げる。あるいはぽいぽいは「どうしてわれわれゾンビがわれわれゾンビのこと考えるのに人間のつくったゾンビ映画参照しなきゃいけないのか」と言い、「人間のゾンビ表象からわれわれ自由になれる日がいつしかくるようにと願って」「ゾンビの視点で描くゾンビ映画」をつくろうとしているのだと宣言する。 『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』東京芸術劇場（2026年8月）［撮影：冨田了平］ 非対称性というキーワードからも明らかなように、ここではゾンビの存在が現実世界におけるさまざまなマイノリティと重ね合わせられている。劇中に登場するゾンビという言葉の大半は、そのまま例えばクィアという言葉に置き換えても──「クィアの視点で描くクィア映画」というようなかたちで──成立するだろう。言及される問題は多岐にわたる。例えばゾンビが登場する映画はすべてがゾンビ映画という括りに入れられてしまうということ。ゾンビは本当は人間と同じように歩くのであって「人間のゾンビ表象」は間違っているということ。残念ながらそんな「人間のゾンビ表象」によってゾンビが「教育」されてしまっている側面もあるということ。しかし「問題は人間の映画監督のゾンビ描写が貧しいってこと」ではなく「ゾンビの映画監督が圧倒的に少なすぎるっていうのが問題のほんとの所在」であるのだということ等々。 そして話題は観客のことにも及ぶ。ゾンビの観客はどれくらいいるのかと。しかもこの問いは、劇場にいる観客に向けて発せられるのだ。さらに舞台上のゾンビたちはおもむろにゾンビメイクを拭い去り、自分たちが「映画を撮りたいゾンビ」を演じる人間の俳優でしかないという身も蓋もない事実を観客に改めて突きつける。そうして明らかになるのは、舞台上にも客席にも、このゾンビについての演劇が上演されている劇場内にゾンビはひとりも存在していないという端的な事実だ。 『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』東京芸術劇場（2026年8月）［撮影：冨田了平］ 『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』東京芸術劇場（2026年8月）［撮影：相模友士郎］ ともすればポリコレ的言説の演説会にもなりかねない（というかそうでなかったとはなかなか言い切れない）この作品が、チャーミングな飽きさせない上演として成立していたのは俳優たちの魅力に負うところが大きいだろう。そのようなかたちで問いを社会へと持ち込めることもまた、演劇の可能性のひとつなのだ。 この『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』という作品は、『消しゴム山』（初演：2019）から『リビングルームのメタモルフォーシス』（初演：2023）へと展開する脱人間中心主義を掲げた岡田の一連の作品のひとつとしても位置づけられるだろう。そのコンセプトは『消しゴム山』では例えば「モノのための演劇」というきわめてラディカルなかたちで実現されていたが、同作では再演を重ねるなかで、アクセシビリティをめぐるさまざまな取り組みも実施されてきたのだった。それは中心とされてきたはずの人間のなかにも周縁化された存在がいるのだという、当然でありながら日本の演劇界においては十分に目が向けられてこなかった事実に改めて目を向ける取り組みでもある。ノン・ネイティブ日本語話者を出演者に迎えた『宇宙船イン・ビトゥイーン号の窓』（初演：2023）もこの系譜に連なる重要な作品だ。 劇場で配布されていた『劇場に置くノート1』に岡田は次のように記していた。「舞台芸術の上演が現状よりももっと、観客の身体やその振る舞いが肯定されている場になる。観客の身体どうしがその存在を肯定し合っているという場になる。そしたらそれはイノベーションだとおもう。どうやったらそれは起こせるだろう」。このような思想は岡田がアーティスティック・ディレクターを務める舞台芸術祭「秋の隕石」のプログラムや体制にも持ち込まれている。2026年の「秋の隕石」は10月9日（金）から11月3日（火）にかけての開催を予定している。 『映画を撮りたいゾンビの演劇』東京芸術劇場（2026年8月）［撮影：冨田了平］ 観賞日：2026/08/12（水） 関連記事 KYOTO EXPERIMENT 2023（前編） チェルフィッチュ『宇宙船イン・ビトゥイーン号の窓』｜高嶋慈：artscapeレビュー（2023年11月15日号） チェルフィッチュ×金氏徹平『消しゴム山』（エクストラ音声「山がつぶやいている」／配信版『消しゴム山は見ている』）｜山﨑健太：artscapeレビュー（2021年04月15日号） 没入するモノたち──チェルフィッチュ×金氏徹平『消しゴム山』｜池田剛介：フォーカス（2019年10月15日号）

items.album: 山川陸｜特別企画展「芳年　激動の時代を生きた鬼才浮世絵師」（中編）

items.body: 会期：2026/08/01〜2026/09/27 会場：水野美術館［長野県］ 公式サイト：https://mizuno-museum.jp/exhibition/2026-08-exhibiton/ （前編より） 展示されていたのは、連作のうち《神奈川 横浜遠景》と《鞠子 名物とろゝ汁》である。注目したいのは後者である。 《鞠子 名物とろゝ汁》（以下、「鞠子」）に描かれた鞠子（丸子）は東海道のなかではもっとも小さい宿場であり、現在の静岡市に位置する。名物であるとろろ汁の看板や茶屋の様子は、「東海道五拾三次之内」（1834）をはじめ歌川広重のさまざまな東海道五十三次に描かれてきた。従来の東海道ものでは、江戸から京都へと向かう方向に連作が組まれているが、東幸を描いた本作では京都から東京へ向かう方向で組まれている。また、宿場のすべてではなく7カ所しか描かれていないことは、それまでの東海道五十三次とはねらいが異なるのだと考えられる。あるいは、やむなく断念したのかはわからない。 「鞠子」は紙を縦使いしており、画面の中央下部3分の1ほどに消失点が据えられた一点透視の構図となっている。画面中央やや上に錦の御旗が掲げられ、それを先頭で担ぐ洋装の兵士、後ろに三列で複数人の兵士が続いている。行進の左右にはとろろ汁の看板がかかった茶屋が並び、その手前には膝をついて平伏しながらも、顔を上げて行進を眺める男女の姿がある。飾りのついた御旗の背景はぽかんとひらけた空で、画面下半分の描き込みとは対照的だ。そして、右上にタイトルとして「東海道名所圖繪」「鞠子 名物とろゝ汁」と縦書きされている★4。 ところで、消失点は前述したように画面下方に位置する。つまり、消失点は錦の御旗ではなく、それを担ぐ兵士の顔付近にある。右肩に御旗を担いでいることから、消失点そのものは肩口のあたりにあり、担ぐ兵士の顔と、その後ろを歩く兵士の顔が消失点を挟むように並んでいる。どの兵士の顔も俯き加減で、町人の顔と同じく簡素な線で描かれている。芳年が多くの作品で描いてきた、歴史に名の残る勇壮な武士、強い意志から行動に出た者の表情とはまったく異なっている。本作と、一般的に想像される芳年の作品イメージには落差がある。 芳年の絵の特徴は、無惨絵に代表される“ショッキングな表現”だけではない。躍動する身体を一時停止したかのようなダイナミックな構図設定と描写力もその特徴だ。歌舞伎における「見得」はパフォーマンスにおいて動きを止めてみせるものだが、芳年は静止した画面に、存在しない前後の時間と運動を思わせる。例えば後年の《芳年武者无類 源牛若丸 熊坂長範》（1883）に見られるように、はためく着物や頭巾、踏みしめる脚や薙刀の柄といったモチーフは、周囲の余白をこの直前／直後に運動して通過していく空間として見せている。また、タイトルや人物名のキャプションといった画面としてのメタ情報も含めて画面が構成されていることは言うまでもない。 このような運動の痕跡と予感で埋め尽くした描き方は、一見静かな画題である晩年の連作「月百姿」（1885-92）でも健在だ。どの画面も激しい運動を描いたものではないが、遠景の月と照らされる近景の関係、また人物の視線や姿勢が持つ動きが余白を埋めている。 本展のポスターにも用いられている《魁題百撰相 駒木根八兵衛》（1868）では、画面を眺める鑑賞者に向かって銃口が向けられている。メタ情報のグラフィック配置も含め、芳年の画面設計は画面内の移動のみならず、画面へ向かう視線にまで向けられている。可視・不可視にかかわらず、芳年の作品に対峙する鑑賞者はこうしたさまざまな運動を辿っている。 しかし、「鞠子」の画面内は運動に満ちているようには見えない。行進に向けられる町民の目線と、行進する兵士の伏し目がちな目線は交わらない。それでも動きとしては画面の手前に向かって彼らは進んでくる。その運動により、錦の御旗はゆっくりと揺れながら前進したことだろう。しかし、画面内唯一の行進という運動は、その手足の運動をもっとも感じさせない正面から構図が取られている。これはやはり、変わりゆく時代、なにかの終焉を象徴する場面であり、ほかの勇壮な作品とは異なる質のものなのだろうか。 （後編へ）※2026年10月7日公開予定 ★4──ジャパンサーチでは単色のものが掲載されているが、本展では多色刷りの錦絵（版元：大橋屋弥七）が展示されていた。特に兵士の洋装は、ほかの連作に比べると落ち着いた淡い色合いであった。筆者は軽度の色弱のため、写真が手元にない状態で色彩描写を行なうことは難しい。色彩が重要な要素であることは理解しつつも、本稿では記述できない点をご容赦いただきたい。 鑑賞日：2026/09/12（土）

items.excerpt: 2016年に発表した『Water Falls Into A Blank』のリイシューが決まり、海外でもまた評価の気運が高まりそうな7FOのニュー・アルバムはEMから。道で拾った石が突如割れたというささやかな記憶の断片から実となった、ストレンジだが妙に人懐っこい音楽は本作でも唯一無二。ニューエイジ的な浮遊感を入口に広がる景色には陶然とするばかり。

items.excerpt: デビュー曲“Lost Boy”のヒットから11年。カナダ人シンガー・ソングライターの5年ぶり3作目。その間に体験した破局をテーマにした内省的なバラードが並ぶが、不思議と優しく癒してくれる。カーリー・レイ・ジェプセンの夫で彼女やベックを手掛けるコールM.G.N.と共に制作。ピアノやウクレレ、ギターの優しい音色と、吐息混じりの歌声が、ふんわり美しく絡み合う。

items.body: Truth must be said from the beginning, I’m not, even a little, objective when it comes to John Coltrane’s last chapter in life and in music. Those two are inseparable in any case. Second truth is that this last period that starts roughly sometime in 1964, prior to A Love Supreme, and ends with his death is my favorite music. He and all his comrades, especially Alice, Pharoah, Rashied and Jimmy managed to create a body of music of transcendence –an ascension for the soul and deep meditation for the mind. My album of choice is this last live recording (where the aforementioned musicians are joined by Juma Santos and Algie DeWitt on percussion), recorded just three months before his death at the Olatunji Center of African Culture in Harlem, N.Y.C. In a quite symbolic move (the place: deep in an African-American neighborhood, the name: African Culture and tradition as a starting point) the music of the players, even though both geographically and in name still black, still jazz but free, is already a new entity. With this recording, one that the sound is not so hi-fi, Coltrane’s sound seems to be in the final stage of the total freedom that Ascension initiated. Listening to the unrelenting growls, howls and their thick wall of sound created by Trane and Pharoah, one could easily comment that the two tracks, Ogunde of almost half an hour and the total reconstruction of My Favorite Things that clocks in thirty four uncontrollably joyous minutes, are pure noise. This ferocious a la Ayler attack by the two locked in reeds brothers, provides a rough field, like a magic carpet flying in the air, for the others to give everything they have. And they have to give a lot to the not so big crowd attending, as their collective struggle to follow or lead at some points, or intertwine with small gestures like the polyrhythmic-not-so-rhythmic barrages by Rashied, the lovingly plucked piano chords by Alice and the even though not always audible, monstrous strength by Jimmy on double bass. Allow me to humbly comment that Coltrane’s music channeled everything in black tradition and went beyond that. He created his own tradition. You also don’t need me to say that this is an amazing recording. One that encapsulates all the stated goals by John Coltrane himself. Total freedom, love, myriads of feelings and a spiritual unity that could be the final Truth. If there’s something to think about, to question, it could be this: where could his music go after this? Did he, before even turning 41, reached a point of no return? @fot.isn Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: Out Of Your Head Records, 2026 Personnel - David Léon: saxophone, flute; Kenny Warren: trumpet; Stephan Crump: bass; Ches Smith: drums. Bassist and composer Stephan Crump, a musician of extraordinary passion and lyricism, put together a crisp, bright new ensemble for his latest outing, Passerine , a work of originals inspired by the various nesting techniques of birds. Relying on a frontline composed of Cuban-American saxophonist and flutist David Léon and trumpeter Kenny Warren, and pairing up beautifully with the resourceful drummer Ches Smith, Crump has something fresh to say. " Stuck " firstly evolves in a 3/4 time signature, displaying a big, round bass sound that shelters sharp unison melody. Léon narrates a story over an arco bass ostinato, while Smith explores toms and cymbal sounds with sagacity. There's a change of pace and texture for Warren's expressive solo, and the interplay between the rhythm team becomes more defiant, leading to a swinging passage before returning to the initial waltzing breeze. " Glide " is executed with a compelling rhythmic quality underneath—Crump incorporating effortless bass pedals, pizzicato routes, and cool grooves that find consistent support in Smith's nicely brushed skins. On flute, Léon stands out, drawing from melodic and harmonic minor modes in his improvisation. " Weavers " and " Twenty-Five " are warm meditative exercises where all members leave flowery scents in the air while rowing in the same direction. The former piece rests on a relaxed bass harmonic conduction that breathes at a challenging tempo, having charismatic, pure-toned unisons running atop. The latter is a shape-shifter that initiates with a sparse bass figure, understated drumming, a pellucid flute whose gentle dance emulates the chirp of birds, and introspective trumpet. Warren and Léon always take maximum advantage of their instruments to create dual melodic lines that feel luminous and often varied in shape. That's the case on " Fly ", a well-balanced 3/4 canvas painted with a certain wry melancholia. Breathable bass and brush work create space and smooth out the environment, culminating in a pulsating bass pedal point at the center of the outro vamp. With sensitive collaborative input from the musicians enlisted, Passerine is a point of departure and an embrace of transformation for Crump. It's also detailed with rigor without abandoning the freedom of creating spontaneously. The composer's sophisticated sound and gracious storytelling are filtered into the album's sequence. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Stuck ► 02 - Glide ► 03 - Weavers

items.body:
Bestards (理想混蛋) are coming back to Singapore.

Following their sold-out show last year, the Taiwanese band will reunite with fans at The Theatre at Mediacorp on 18 December, 7:30PM. Presented by CK Star Entertainment, 《不是因为天气晴朗才见面》 (BESTORY) will also stop at Zepp Kuala Lumpur on 21 November before heading to Singapore.

Formed in 2017, Bestards comprise vocalist Kidding (鸡丁), guitarists Jerry (阿哲) and Dillion (建廷), and drummer Look (可沛). Their heartfelt songwriting has earned them a devoted following of “Little Bastards” (小混蛋), alongside a growing presence on Taiwan’s live music circuit.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by CK Star Entertainment SG 🇸🇬 (@ckstar.sg)

The band’s best-known songs include ‘不是因为天气晴朗才爱你’ and ‘离开的一路上’ (‘Farewell’), which have surpassed 96 million and 58 million Spotify streams respectively. Bestards were also Spotify’s most-streamed band in Taiwan in 2024.

Their Singapore return follows the September release of their fourth full-length album, 偶像包袱 (MIMICRY). Arriving three years after their previous record, the album explores adulthood through questions of responsibility, expectations, identity, and life choices, expanding beyond the youth and romance that shaped their earlier work.

Among its tracks is ‘最后一个谎’ (‘One Last Bouquet’), written and composed by Kidding. Its music video crossed one million YouTube views within four days of release.

For the Singapore edition of BESTORY, fans can look forward to a mix of familiar favourites and new songs from MIMICRY.

Tickets go on sale on 13 October at 12PM SGT via BookMyShow, with prices as follows:

VIP: SGD208

CAT 1: SGD158

CAT 2: SGD138

CAT 3: SGD118

CAT 4: SGD88

Prices exclude booking fees. VIP tickets include a signed postcard and a 1:10 group photo.

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”
